blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An analyst counts the plans of a one-budget selection with a table that keeps a count for every $10k of budget. Finance now wants every cost and the budget kept to the dollar. What happens to the table?

options.text: It keeps its length, since its length follows the number of projects
options.says: The table has one entry per budget amount; the projects set how many passes run over it.

options.text: It becomes 10,000 times longer, since its length follows the budget's size
options.says: Right: $10k units to dollars is a factor of 10,000 in the number of budget amounts: pseudo-polynomial work.

options.text: It becomes 4 entries longer, since its length follows the budget's digits
options.says: The work grows with the budget's size as a number, not with how many digits it takes to write.

options.text: It becomes 1,000 times longer, since its length follows the costs in $k
options.says: The table counted in $10k units, so going to dollars multiplies its length by 10,000, not 1,000.

origin.section: A Table Over Budget Amounts Counts Plans Without Listing Them

questions.stem: A depth-first search over 30 yes/no choices visits 2,000 nodes on a portfolio where the full tree has about two billion. Which step of the search let it leave out the rest?

options.text: Skipping each project that no longer fits in the budget left
options.says: That check saved about half the tree in the lesson's run, not almost all of it.

options.text: Stopping the search once the first allowed plan is found
options.says: The search keeps going after its first plan; it only skips subtrees it can prove are no better.

options.text: Skipping each node whose ceiling cannot beat the best plan so far
options.says: Right: the LP bound of what is left proves the whole subtree cannot win, so it is skipped.

options.text: Sorting the projects so the best value per dollar comes first
options.says: The order helps the bound find good plans early, but by itself it skips no node.

origin.section: A Search Tree With a Bound Visits a Sliver of the Plans

questions.stem: Model A has 2,000 binaries and an LP bound within 0.01% of its best plan. Model B has 40 binaries and equality rows that the point with every variable at 0.5 satisfies. Which is likely to need the larger search?

options.text: B, since its relaxation rules out almost nothing at a node
options.says: Right: a relaxation that is satisfied nearly everywhere proves nothing, so the search must branch deep.

options.text: A, since its tree has far more nodes at the bottom level
options.says: The bottom level counts plans, not the nodes a bounded search visits; GridCap medium needed one node.

options.text: A, since a bound that close leaves more nodes to explore
options.says: A close bound lets the search skip more, not less.

options.text: B, since a MILP solver refuses rows that are equalities
options.says: Equality rows are ordinary MILP rows; the puzzle's are accepted and solved, just slowly.

origin.section: Size Does Not Decide Difficulty; the Bound's Strength Does
